The release should define nested memory as explicitly scoped, addressable state rather than an implicit global context. - Dynamic providers need a stable contract for discovery, selection, capability metadata, authentication, deadlines, retries, and graceful fallback. - Provider choice and memory resolution should be observable through traceable IDs, source/provider attribution, latency, and failure reasons. - Backward compatibility requires deterministic defaults for existing callers and an opt-in path for nested memory and dynamic-provider behavior. ## Risks or open questions - Clarify precedence when parent and child memory disagree, including deletion, redaction, and tenant isolation. - Confirm provider trust boundaries, secret handling, schema/version negotiation, and behavior when a provider disappears at runtime. - Define rollout gates, metrics, and a kill switch before enabling dynamic routing broadly. ## Recommendations or next steps - Publish a minimal API contract with typed memory paths, provider capability negotiation, deadlines, and typed errors. - Preserve deterministic, backward-compatible defaults for existing callers; expand routing only after conformance tests, canaries, and rollback controls demonstrate safe behavior. ## Key evidence - Nested memory should be modeled as typed, addressable paths with explicit scope—not as implicit global context. - Dynamic providers need consistent discovery and selection semantics, capability metadata, authentication, deadlines, retries, typed errors, and graceful fallback. - Provider selection and memory resolution must be traceable through IDs, source/provider attribution, latency, and failure reasons. - Existing callers require deterministic defaults and an explicit opt-in path for nested-memory and dynamic-provider behavior. - A minimal API contract plus conformance coverage should test nesting, precedence, provider churn, retries, idempotency, and fallback determinism. ## Risks or cautions - Resolve parent/child precedence, including deletion and redaction semantics, before broad enablement. - Establish tenant isolation, provider trust boundaries, secret handling, and schema/version negotiation. - Define behavior when a provider disappears or changes at runtime; dynamic routing must fail safely rather than silently alter results. - Set rollout gates, success metrics, audit visibility, and a kill switch before production expansion. ## Next actions - Publish the typed API contract for memory paths, capability negotiation, deadlines, fallback, and typed errors. - Implement conformance tests covering nesting, precedence, retries, idempotency, provider churn, and deterministic fallback. - Add audit logs and dashboards for routing decisions, resolution sources, latency, and failures. - Launch a small canary behind feature flags with documented rollback criteria; retain legacy defaults unless explicitly enabled.
